Hedersett Usurps Power

The order reached the ministries before the presidium had time to discuss it. Citing the country's armed split, Rufus Hedersett concentrated leadership of the Party government in his own hands. Orders to the troops, appointments and supply decisions must now pass through his office. Elections have been postponed indefinitely.

At the meeting, the secretary read out the document as already in force. Those who objected were invited to submit their comments in writing; their signatures were not required. By evening, district chancelleries had received new order templates and a demand to confirm their obedience.

Official radio called it a temporary measure to preserve the state. Hedersett's opponents called it usurpation. As fronts formed beyond the capital, the Party apparatus received a single master.
The orders have already been sent.
